_**User (2026-10-08 05:16:22Z)**_

I am now working on the issue:

A user visits their Event Types page, where each event card displays a star icon. Clicking an empty star marks it as a favorite and immediately moves the card to a dedicated Favorites section at the top of the screen. Clicking a highlighted star removes it from favorites and places the card back into the regular list below. The user can continue to rearrange regular events however they like.

I have the DI wiring completed, but verify to make sure it is complete

```text
    13	  async create({ userId, eventTypeId }: EventTypeFavoriteKey): Promise<void> {
    14	    await this.prismaClient.eventTypeFavorite.createMany({
    15	      data: [{ userId, eventTypeId }],
    16	      skipDuplicates: true,
    17	    });
    18	  }
    19	
    20	  // removes a favorite
    21	  // deleteMany doesn't throw when the row is already gone, unlike delete
    22	  async delete({ userId, eventTypeId }: EventTypeFavoriteKey): Promise<void> {
    23	    await this.prismaClient.eventTypeFavorite.deleteMany({
    24	      where: { userId, eventTypeId },
    25	    });
    26	  }
    27	
    28	  // gets a list of all event IDs favorited by the user
    29	  // only grabs events belonging to the user
    30	  // puts newest favorites first
    31	  async findEventTypeIdsByUserId(userId: number): Promise<number[]> {
    32	    const favorites = await this.prismaClient.eventTypeFavorite.findMany({
    33	      where: { userId },
    34	      select: { eventTypeId: true },
    35	      orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" },
    36	    });
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-08 05:20:39Z)**_

Yes. The database table, the repository and the DI container are all in place, and the tests confirm they work. No tRPC code calls them yet, so the frontend has no way to reach them.

The tRPC layer needs two things:

1. **Turning a favorite on or off:** an endpoint the star calls that adds or removes a favorite for the logged-in user. Before writing anything, it should check that the user can actually access that event type. Otherwise anyone could favorite any event type ID.
2. **Reading favorites:** the Event Types page has to know which cards are favorited. You could add a separate query, or have the existing event types list query also return whether each card is a favorite. The second avoids an extra request and keeps the two lists in sync.

After that, the frontend work is the star button on each card, plus a Favorites section at the top that updates immediately when a star is clicked.

That access check is business logic, so the repo's rules would put it in a service rather than the repository. A small `EventTypeFavoriteService` would need its own token, module and container. Putting the check directly in the tRPC handler is also acceptable for something this small.

```text
    .use(async ({ ctx, input, next }) => {
      const id = input.eventTypeId ?? input.id;

      const event = await ctx.prisma.eventType.findUnique({
        where: { id },
        select: {
          id: true,
          userId: true,
          teamId: true,
          users: {
            select: {
              id: true,
            },
          },
          team: {
            select: {
              members: {
                select: {
                  userId: true,
                },
              },
            },
          },
        },
      });

      if (!event) {
        throw new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND" });
      }

      // Check if user has permission to access/modify this event
      if (!event.teamId) {
        // Personal event - must be owner or assigned user
        if (event.userId !== ctx.user.id && !event.users.find((user) => user.id === ctx.user.id)) {
          throw new TRPCError({
            code: "FORBIDDEN",
            message: `Permission required: ${permission}`,
          });
        }
      } else {
        // Team event - check PBAC/fallback permissions
        const permissionCheckService = new PermissionCheckService();
        const hasPermission = await permissionCheckService.checkPermission({
          userId: ctx.user.id,
          teamId: event.teamId,
          permission,
          fallbackRoles,
        });

        if (!hasPermission) {
          throw new TRPCError({
            code: "FORBIDDEN",
            message: `Permission required: ${permission}`,
          });
        }
      }

      // Validate that assigned users are allowed
      if (input.users && input.users.length > 0) {
        const isAllowed = (() => {
          if (event.team) {
            const allTeamMembers = event.team.members.map((member) => member.userId);
            return input.users?.every((userId: number) => allTeamMembers.includes(userId)) ?? true;
          }
          return input.users?.every((userId: number) => userId === ctx.user.id) ?? true;
        })();

        if (!isAllowed) {
          console.warn(
            `User ${ctx.user.id} attempted to assign event ${event.id} to users ${input.users.join(", ")}.`
          );
          throw new TRPCError({
            code: "FORBIDDEN",
            message: "Cannot assign event to users outside of team membership",
          });
        }
      }

      return next();
    });
};
```

```text
  private readonly hashedLinkRepository: HashedLinkRepository;

  private normalizeLinkInput(input: string | HashedLinkInputType): NormalizedLink {
    return typeof input === "string"
      ? { link: input, expiresAt: null }

          link: input.link,
```

```text
import { prisma } from "@calcom/prisma";
import type { TrpcSessionUser } from "@calcom/trpc/server/types";

import { TRPCError } from "@trpc/server";

import type { TEventTypeOrderInputSchema } from "./eventTypeOrder.schema";

type EventTypeOrderOptions = {
  ctx: {
    user: NonNullable<TrpcSessionUser>;
  };
  input: TEventTypeOrderInputSchema;
};

export const eventTypeOrderHandler = async ({ ctx, input }: EventTypeOrderOptions) => {
  const { user } = ctx;

  const allEventTypes = await prisma.eventType.findMany({
    select: {
      id: true,
    },
    where: {
      id: {
        in: input.ids,
      },
      OR: [
        {
          userId: user.id,
        },
        {
          users: {
            some: {
              id: user.id,
            },
          },
        },
        {
          team: {
            members: {
              some: {
                userId: user.id,
              },
            },
          },
        },
      ],
    },
  });
  const allEventTypeIds = new Set(allEventTypes.map((type) => type.id));
  if (input.ids.some((id) => !allEventTypeIds.has(id))) {
    throw new TRPCError({
      code: "UNAUTHORIZED",
    });
  }
  await Promise.all(
    input.ids.reverse().map((id, position) => {
      return prisma.eventType.update({
        where: {
          id,
        },
        data: {
          position,
        },
      });
    })
  );
};
import { bindModuleToClassOnToken, createModule, type ModuleLoader } from "@calcom/features/di/di";
import { DI_TOKENS } from "@calcom/features/di/tokens";
import { MembershipRepository } from "@calcom/features/membership/repositories/MembershipRepository";
import { moduleLoader as prismaModuleLoader } from "@calcom/features/di/modules/Prisma";

export const membershipRepositoryModule = createModule();
const token = DI_TOKENS.MEMBERSHIP_REPOSITORY;
const moduleToken = DI_TOKENS.MEMBERSHIP_REPOSITORY_MODULE;
const loadModule = bindModuleToClassOnToken({
  module: membershipRepositoryModule,
  moduleToken,
  token,
  classs: MembershipRepository,
  dep: prismaModuleLoader,
});

export const moduleLoader: ModuleLoader = {
  token,
  loadModule,
};
```

# Service vs. handler for the favorites access check

## Needed whichever option you pick

**1. The access rule.** A user should be able to favorite any event type that appears on their page:
- one they own,
- one they're assigned to,
- a team event type for a team they belong to.

[eventTypeOrder.handler.ts:18-46](packages/trpc/server/routers/loggedInViewer/eventTypeOrder.handler.ts#L18-L46) already uses exactly this rule for reordering, so copy it.

**Don't use `createEventPbacProcedure` for this.** Its team branch calls a `PermissionCheckService` that this fork stubbed to always return `true` ([util.ts:15-20](packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/eventTypes/util.ts#L15-L20)). Any logged-in user would pass for *any* team event, including teams they aren't in. And even if it worked, it's meant to check edit rights, which is the wrong question for starring.

**2. A new repository method for the access check.** Neither option can query Prisma directly from the handler or service. The closest existing method is `findByIdWithUserAccess` ([eventTypeRepository.ts:536](packages/features/eventtypes/repositories/eventTypeRepository.ts#L536)), but it falls short in two ways:
- It ignores team membership, so team members who aren't hosts would be refused.
- It has no `select`, so it fetches every column.

Add something like `existsWithUserAccess({ id, userId }): Promise<boolean>` to `EventTypeRepository` with the `eventTypeOrder` rule, plus a unit test. This is also what stops a nonexistent ID from reaching `createMany` and failing on the foreign key.

**3. Input shape.** Use `{ eventTypeId: number, isFavorite: boolean }` instead of a bare "toggle". Setting an explicit value means a double click or a retry can't flip the star back. It also fits optimistic UI updates, and your `skipDuplicates`/`deleteMany` choices already make both directions safe to repeat.

**4. The tRPC entry.** Either way you add `setFavorite.schema.ts`, a handler file, and an `authedProcedure` entry in [_router.ts](packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/eventTypes/_router.ts).

## Option A: an `EventTypeFavoriteService`

**What it entails** (about 7 code files):

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `eventtypes/service/EventTypeFavoriteService.ts` | The business logic. Goes in `service/` (singular), where `EventTypeService` already lives. |
| `eventtypes/di/tokens.ts` | 2 new tokens: the service and its module. |
| `eventtypes/di/EventTypeFavoriteService.module.ts` | A `depsMap` with your favorites repository module and `di/modules/EventType`. |
| `eventtypes/di/EventTypeFavoriteService.container.ts` | `getEventTypeFavoriteService()` |
| `eventtypes/service/EventTypeFavoriteService.test.ts` | Tests with fake repositories, no database needed. |
| `setFavorite.schema.ts` and `setFavorite.handler.ts` | A thin handler that only passes the request to the service. |
| `_router.ts` | One entry. |

The core of the service would look roughly like this:

```ts
async setFavorite({ userId, eventTypeId, isFavorite }: SetFavoriteInput): Promise<void> {
  const canAccess = await this.deps.eventTypeRepository.existsWithUserAccess({ id: eventTypeId, userId });
  if (!canAccess) throw ErrorWithCode.Factory.NotFound(`Event type ${eventTypeId} not found`);

  if (isFavorite) {
    await this.deps.eventTypeFavoriteRepository.create({ userId, eventTypeId });
    return;
  }
  await this.deps.eventTypeFavoriteRepository.delete({ userId, eventTypeId });
}
```

Use `NotFound` rather than `Forbidden` here, so the error doesn't reveal that an event type ID exists. `errorConversionMiddleware` is already on `authedProcedure`, so `ErrorWithCode` becomes a `TRPCError` automatically. The service would also own `listFavoriteIds(userId)` for the read side.

**One DI catch:** the `EventType` module ([di/modules/EventType.ts](packages/features/di/modules/EventType.ts)) doesn't load Prisma itself. That's why `EventTypeService.container.ts` loads `prismaModule` by hand. Your service works without that only because the favorites repository module's `dep` happens to load Prisma into the same container. To make it explicit, either add the manual load in the container, as `EventTypeService` does, or add a comment saying why it isn't needed.

**Pros**
- Follows the repo rules: business logic lives in services, handlers stay thin, and DI gives you both repositories without new repository containers.
- The access rule is the only real logic in this feature, and here it gets plain unit tests with no tRPC context to mock.
- API v2 or the read side can reuse it later through a re-export in `platform-libraries`.

**Cons**
- Three more files than Option B, plus more wiring to review.
- With the repository method, its test and the handler, this sits right at the 10-file PR limit. You can split it: PR 1 is the repository method, the service and its DI; PR 2 is the tRPC endpoint.

## Option B: the check inside the tRPC handler

**What it entails** (about 4 code files):
- `setFavorite.schema.ts`
- `setFavorite.handler.ts`, which runs the access check and then calls `getEventTypeFavoriteRepository()`
- the `_router.ts` entry
- the repository method and its test

There's no container for `EventTypeRepository`, so the handler would build it directly with `new EventTypeRepository(ctx.prisma)`. [getEventTypesFromGroup.handler.ts:49](packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/eventTypes/getEventTypesFromGroup.handler.ts#L49) already does this, but it's the "manual instantiation" mistake the DI rule names. The alternative is a new repository container, which brings the file count back up.

**Pros**
- Fewer files, and fits in one PR.
- Matches what most handlers in this router actually do today: `delete` and `eventTypeOrder` both check access inline.

**Cons**
- Puts business logic in the tRPC layer, against `CLAUDE.md` and the repository-pattern rules. A reviewer applying `quality-thorough-code-review.md` would likely flag it.
- Testing the access rule means building a tRPC `ctx` and mocking around it.
- API v2 can't reuse it, so moving it into a service later is exactly the follow-up PR the repo's rules warn tends not to happen.

## Recommendation

I'd go with **Option A**. You've already built the harder part, the repository DI, so the extra cost is three small files. In return, the one piece of logic that protects the data gets real unit tests and sits where the repo's rules expect it. Option B only saves real effort if you're tight on time, and it adds a known pattern violation.

## Separate decision: the read side

This applies under either option. The page loads event types 10 at a time, ordered by `position` ([getEventTypesFromGroup.handler.ts:69-79](packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/eventTypes/getEventTypesFromGroup.handler.ts#L69-L79)).

If you only add an `isFavorite` flag and split the list in the browser, a favorite on page 3 won't appear in the Favorites section until the user scrolls that far. A separate `listFavorites` query that feeds the Favorites section avoids this, with the regular list leaving out favorited IDs. That also keeps reordering limited to regular events, which is what the issue asks for.

```text
import { ErrorCode } from "@calcom/lib/errorCodes";

export class ErrorWithCode extends Error {
  code: ErrorCode;
  data?: Record<string, unknown>;
  constructor(code: ErrorCode, message?: string, data?: Record<string, unknown>) {
    super(message);
    this.code = code;
    this.data = data;
  }
  static get Factory() {
    return new Proxy(ErrorWithCode, {
      get(_, prop: string) {
        if (prop in ErrorCode) {
          const code = ErrorCode[prop as keyof typeof ErrorCode];
          return (message?: string, data?: Record<string, unknown>) => new ErrorWithCode(code, message, data);
        }
        throw new Error(`Unknown error code: ${prop}`);
      },
    }) as unknown as Record<
      keyof typeof ErrorCode,
      (message?: string, data?: Record<string, unknown>) => ErrorWithCode
    >;
  }
}

/**
 * Converts unknown error types to Error objects.
 *
 * @deprecated For server-side code, use `getServerErrorFromUnknown` from `@calcom/lib/server/getServerErrorFromUnknown` instead.
 * This function should only be used in client-side or isomorphic code (React components, shared utilities).
 *
 * Use this function when:
 * - You're in a React component that runs on the client
 * - You're in shared/isomorphic code that cannot import server-only dependencies
 * - You only need a basic Error object without HTTP status code mapping
 *
 * For server-side error handling (API routes, tRPC handlers, webhooks), use `getServerErrorFromUnknown`
 * which provides proper HTTP status code mapping, error redaction, and handles Zod/Prisma/Stripe errors.
 *
 * @param cause - The unknown error to convert
 * @returns An Error object with optional statusCode and code properties
 */
export function getErrorFromUnknown(cause: unknown): Error & { statusCode?: number; code?: string } {
  if (cause instanceof Error) {
    return cause;
  }
  if (typeof cause === "string") {
    // @ts-ignore https://github.com/tc39/proposal-error-cause - must use @ts-ignore because different packages have different TS lib targets
    return new Error(cause, { cause });
```

```text
// Copied from `TRPC_ERROR_CODE_KEY` from `@trpc/server/unstable-core-do-not-import`
type TRPCErrorCode =
  | "PARSE_ERROR"
  | "BAD_REQUEST"
  | "INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR"
  | "NOT_IMPLEMENTED"
  | "UNAUTHORIZED"
  | "FORBIDDEN"
  | "NOT_FOUND"
  | "METHOD_NOT_SUPPORTED"
  | "TIMEOUT"
  | "CONFLICT"
  | "PRECONDITION_FAILED"
  | "PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE"
  | "UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT"
  | "TOO_MANY_REQUESTS"
  | "CLIENT_CLOSED_REQUEST";

export function httpStatusToTrpcCode(status: number): TRPCErrorCode {
  switch (status) {
    case 400:
      return "BAD_REQUEST";
    case 401:
      return "UNAUTHORIZED";
    case 403:
      return "FORBIDDEN";
    case 404:
      return "NOT_FOUND";
    case 405:
      return "METHOD_NOT_SUPPORTED";
    case 408:
      return "TIMEOUT";
    case 409:
      return "CONFLICT";
    case 412:
      return "PRECONDITION_FAILED";
    case 413:
      return "PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE";
    case 422:
      return "UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT";
    case 429:
      return "TOO_MANY_REQUESTS";
    case 499:
      return "CLIENT_CLOSED_REQUEST";
    case 501:
      return "NOT_IMPLEMENTED";
    default:
      return "INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR";
  }
}
```

```text
export type ModuleLoader = { token: string | symbol; loadModule: (container: Container) => void };

/**
 * A type-safe alternative to module.bind(token).toClass(classs, deps) that automatically ensures that all dependencies required by the Class are provided.
 * It assumes that dependencies are passed to the constructor as an object map(e.g. new MyService(deps))
 *
 * @returns A function that can be used to load the dependencies into the container automatically.
 */
// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any
export function bindModuleToClassOnToken<TClass extends new (deps: any) => any>({
  module,
  token,
  classs,
  depsMap,
  moduleToken,
}: {
  module: Module;
  moduleToken: string | symbol;
  token: string | symbol;
  classs: TClass;
  depsMap: Record<
    // eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any
    keyof (TClass extends new (deps: infer TDeps) => any ? TDeps : never),
    ModuleLoader
  >;
}): (container: Container) => void;

/**
 * A type-safe alternative to module.bind(token).toClass(classs, deps) that automatically ensures that all dependencies required by the Class are provided.
 * It assumes that there is a single dependency, passed as argument to the constructor
 *
 * @returns A function that can be used to load the dependencies into the container automatically.
 */
// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any
export function bindModuleToClassOnToken<TClass extends new (deps: any) => any>({
  module,
  token,
  classs,
  dep,
  moduleToken,
}: {
  module: Module;
  moduleToken: string | symbol;
  token: string | symbol;
  classs: TClass;
  dep: ModuleLoader;
}): (container: Container) => void;

/**
 * A type-safe alternative to module.bind(token).toClass(classs, deps) that automatically ensures that all dependencies required by the Class are provided.
 * @returns A function that can be used to load the dependencies into the container automatically.
 */
// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any
export function bindModuleToClassOnToken<TClass extends new (deps: any) => any>({
  module,
  token,
  classs,
  depsMap,
  dep,
  moduleToken,
}: {
  module: Module;
  moduleToken: string | symbol;
  token: string | symbol;
  classs: TClass;
  /**
   * When the constructor of the class accept deps as the argument which is a Record of many dependencies
   */
  depsMap?: Record<
    // eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any
    keyof (TClass extends new (deps: infer TDeps) => any ? TDeps : never),
    ModuleLoader
  >;
  /**
   * When the constructor of the class accept a single dependency and is the only argument to constructor.
   */
  dep?: ModuleLoader;
}) {
  if (dep && depsMap) {
    throw new Error(
      "Cannot provide both 'dep' and 'depsMap'. Use 'dep' for single dependency or 'depsMap' for multiple dependencies."
    );
  }

  if (!dep && !depsMap) {
    throw new Error(
      "Must provide either 'dep' for single dependency or 'depsMap' for multiple dependencies."
    );
  }

  if (dep) {
    module.bind(token).toClass(classs, [dep.token]);
  } else if (depsMap) {
    const depsObject = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(depsMap).map(([key, value]) => [key, value.token]));
    module.bind(token).toClass(classs, depsObject);
  }

  return function loadModule(container: Container) {
    container.load(moduleToken, module);

    if (dep) {
      dep.loadModule(container);
    } else if (depsMap) {
      for (const key in depsMap) {
        const loadModule = depsMap[key as keyof typeof depsMap].loadModule;
        loadModule(container);
      }
    }
  };
}
export { createContainer, createModule, type Container, type Module, type ResolveFunction };
```

````markdown
Service core (shape only; exact lines get approved in step 4):
```ts
async setFavorite({ userId, eventTypeId, isFavorite }: SetFavoriteInput): Promise<void> {
  if (!isFavorite) {
    await this.deps.eventTypeFavoriteRepository.delete({ userId, eventTypeId });
    return;
  }
  const hasAccess = await this.deps.eventTypeRepository.existsWithUserAccess({ id: eventTypeId, userId });
  if (!hasAccess) throw ErrorWithCode.Factory.NotFound(`Event type ${eventTypeId} not found`);
  await this.deps.eventTypeFavoriteRepository.create({ userId, eventTypeId });
}
```

**Checkpoint:** run the verification below before moving to PR 2.
````

## Step 1: Add `existsWithUserAccess` to `EventTypeRepository`

**File:** [eventTypeRepository.ts](packages/features/eventtypes/repositories/eventTypeRepository.ts)

**Where:** after the closing `}` of `findByIdWithUserAccess` at [line 543](packages/features/eventtypes/repositories/eventTypeRepository.ts#L543). The existing methods aren't changed.

```ts
544  
545    async existsWithUserAccess({ id, userId }: { id: number; userId: number }): Promise<boolean> {
546      const eventType = await this.prismaClient.eventType.findFirst({
547        where: {
548          id,
549          OR: [
550            { userId },
551            { users: { some: { id: userId } } },
552            { hosts: { some: { userId } } },
553            { team: { members: { some: { userId, accepted: true } } } },
554          ],
555        },
556        select: { id: true },
557      });
558      return !!eventType;
559    }
```

**Line by line:**

- **544:** a blank line separating it from `findByIdWithUserAccess`, the same spacing as every other method in this class.
- **545:** the method signature.
  - `async` because it waits on a database query.
  - **Name:** `existsWithUserAccess` follows the repository naming rules: no entity name in it (not `eventTypeExists...`), and it says what it returns, not who uses it (not `canFavorite`). That keeps it reusable by anything else that needs "can this user see this event type?".
  - **Parameters:** it takes one object, `{ id, userId }`, rather than two positional numbers, matching `findByIdWithUserAccess` right above it. With positional numbers, swapping `id` and `userId` would compile fine and quietly check the wrong thing. Named fields make that mistake hard to make.
  - **Return type:** `Promise<boolean>`. The service only needs yes or no, so returning a boolean means no database row shape leaks out of the repository. This follows the rule that Prisma types stay inside repositories.
- **546:** runs the query.
  - `this.prismaClient` is the client injected through the constructor at [line 82](packages/features/eventtypes/repositories/eventTypeRepository.ts#L82), which is what lets the DI container supply it and tests fake it.
  - It uses `findFirst` rather than `findUnique`. `findUnique` is meant for lookups by unique fields; `findByIdWithUserAccess` gets away with adding `OR` to it only through a Prisma extension. `findFirst` accepts any `where` without relying on that, and since `id` is the primary key it still returns at most one row.
- **547-548:** `where: { id, ...}` is short for `id: id`, so the row must be this exact event type. All the conditions in a `where` must be true together.
- **549:** `OR: [...]` means the user needs to match **at least one** of the four access paths below, in addition to the `id` match.
- **550:** `{ userId }` matches when the user **owns** the event type, which is the case for personal event types.
- **551:** `{ users: { some: { id: userId } } }` matches when the user is **assigned** to it through the `users` relation. `some` means at least one related row matches. Managed or child event types for a user can be linked this way.
- **552:** `{ hosts: { some: { userId } } }` matches when the user is a **host** on a team event type (round-robin or collective). `findByIdWithUserAccess` includes this clause, so it's here for consistency. On its own it's mostly redundant with line 553, since hosts must be team members.
- **553:** `{ team: { members: { some: { userId, accepted: true } } } }` matches when the event type belongs to a team the user is an **accepted** member of. This is the clause `findByIdWithUserAccess` lacks. Without it, a regular team member couldn't star a team event type they can see on the page.
  - `accepted: true` excludes people with a pending invite. `eventTypeOrder.handler.ts` leaves this out, but someone who hasn't accepted shouldn't get team access.
  - For a personal event type, `team` is `null`, so this clause just doesn't match. It never errors.
- **556:** `select: { id: true }` asks Postgres for only the `id` column. We only need to know whether a row exists, so this keeps the query light. It also follows the repo rule to use `select` and never fetch whole rows; compare `findByIdWithUserAccess`, which fetches every column.
- **557:** closes the query call.
- **558:** `!!eventType` turns the result into a real boolean. `findFirst` returns the row object (`{ id: 42 }`) or `null`; the first `!` turns that into `false` or `true`, and the second flips it back. So a found row gives `true` and `null` gives `false`. This is what keeps the return type `Promise<boolean>` honest.
- **559:** closes the method.

**What it doesn't do:** it doesn't throw or decide what happens when access is denied. Deciding that is business logic, so it belongs in the service (step 4). The repository just answers the question.

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-08 05:47:05Z)**_

Yes, with one detail: it checks both things in a **single query** and gives back **one** answer.

- **`true`**: the event type exists **and** the user has access to it. "Access" means one of the four paths: they own it, they're assigned to it, they host it, or they're an accepted member of its team.
- **`false`**: either the event type doesn't exist, **or** it exists but the user has no access. The function can't tell these two apart, and that's on purpose.

This works because of how the `where` clause is built. It looks for a row matching `id` **and** at least one access path, so a nonexistent ID and someone else's event type both find no row and both return `false`.

That's why the service in step 4 will throw `NotFound` in both cases. If we had separate "doesn't exist" and "no access" answers, a user could probe IDs and learn which event types exist on other accounts. Merging them means the error gives nothing away.

One small wording point about "see it": the four paths match the event types that appear on that user's Event Types page. So the function really answers "is this one of *my* event types, personal or team?" It doesn't answer "can this user book it?" Anyone can book public event types, but that's not what this checks.

**Second test (22-28): a found row means `true`.**

- **23:** the fake database returns a row.
- **25:** this time we keep the result.
- **27:** `toBe(true)` uses strict equality (`===`). That's exactly why line 558 of the method uses `!!`: if the method returned the row object `{ id: 42 }` instead of `true`, this test would fail. It checks that we really return a boolean, not just a truthy value.

**Third test (30-36): no row means `false`.**

- **30:** the name spells out that `false` covers both cases, nonexistent or no access, which documents the behavior you asked about.
- **31:** `mockResolvedValue(null)` imitates Prisma finding no matching row, which is what Postgres returns in both cases.
- **35:** `toBe(false)` checks that we return a real `false`, not `null`.

**Why these don't hit a real database:** these are unit tests of the repository's *contract*: what query it sends and how it turns the result into a boolean. Whether Postgres actually evaluates the `OR` correctly is Prisma's job. A full database check could be added to the integration test file later, but it isn't needed for coverage.

**File:** [tokens.ts](packages/features/eventtypes/di/tokens.ts). Two lines go after line 5; nothing else changes.

```ts
1  export const EVENT_TYPE_DI_TOKENS = {
2    EVENT_TYPE_SERVICE: Symbol("EventTypeService"),
3    EVENT_TYPE_SERVICE_MODULE: Symbol("EventTypeServiceModule"),
4    EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_REPOSITORY: Symbol("EventTypeFavoriteRepository"),
5    EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_REPOSITORY_MODULE: Symbol("EventTypeFavoriteRepositoryModule"),

8  };
```

**Line 6: `EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE`** is the key for the service **instance**.
- The container is basically a lookup table: "for this key, give me this object." `getEventTypeFavoriteService()` in step 7 asks the container for this key.
- **Why a `Symbol` and not a string:** every `Symbol(...)` is unique, even if two have the same label. If another feature also made a token called `"EventTypeFavoriteService"`, the two would still never collide. The text in the parentheses is just a label that shows up when debugging, for example in error messages.

**Line 7: `EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE_MODULE`** is the key for the **module**, the recipe that says "build an `EventTypeFavoriteService` and give it these two repositories."
- `getEventTypeFavoriteService()` reloads the recipe every time it's called, as the existing pattern does. The container files the recipe under this key, so loading it again just replaces the same entry instead of piling up duplicates.

**Why both tokens go here and not in the global [di/tokens.ts](packages/features/di/tokens.ts):** that file already includes this whole object at [line 77](packages/features/di/tokens.ts#L77) (`...EVENT_TYPE_DI_TOKENS`). So `DI_TOKENS.EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE` becomes available everywhere without touching the shared file. This is the same thing you did for the repository tokens on lines 4–5.

**Naming:** both follow the existing pattern in this file. The pair for the repository is `X` and `X_MODULE`; the service gets `EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE` and `EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE_MODULE`.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-08 06:02:32Z)**_

Fair question. There are three DI pieces here, and step 3 only adds one kind: **tokens**, not a container. Here's what each piece does and which ones each class really needs.

| Piece | What it is | Repository | Service |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Token** | A unique name tag: "the thing called X" | ✅ you made it | step 3 |
| **Module** | A recipe: "to build X, use class Y with dependencies Z" | ✅ you made it | step 6 |
| **Container** | The entry point that follows the recipes and hands you a built X | ✅ you made it | step 7 |

**Why the service needs its own token and module:** the container can only build things it has a name and a recipe for. The service is a different object from the repository, with a different recipe: "build `EventTypeFavoriteService` and give it the favorites repository *and* `EventTypeRepository`." So it needs its own token and its own module. The service's recipe then *points to* the repository's recipe (`depsMap` in step 6). That's how the container knows to build the repository first and pass it in.

**Do you need both containers? Not really. This is where your instinct is right.** A container is only needed for something code fetches *directly*. Once the service exists:
- The tRPC handlers will call `getEventTypeFavoriteService()`. They never touch the repository directly, because the service does that.
- The repository is still built, but only *inside* the service's container, through its module. It doesn't need its own container for that.
- The only remaining caller of `getEventTypeFavoriteRepository()` is your integration test ([EventTypeFavoriteRepository.integration-test.ts:40](packages/features/eventtypes/repositories/EventTypeFavoriteRepository.integration-test.ts#L40)).

The codebase works the same way elsewhere. `hashedLink/di/` has a `HashedLinkRepository.module.ts` but **no repository container**; only the service gets fetched from outside.

So you have two choices for the repository container:
- **Keep it.** It costs nothing, and your integration test uses it to check the repository's wiring against a real database.
- **Delete it** and change the integration test to build the repository directly. That's one less file, but the test would no longer exercise the wiring, and the repo's rules say to ask before deleting files.

I'd keep it, since it's already merged and tested. Either way, the service still needs its token, module and container (steps 3, 6, 7). Without them, the tRPC handler has no way to get the service.

Do you want to approve step 3 as shown, or decide about the repository container first?

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-08 06:08:59Z)**_

They're names for **two different objects**, and the container needs a separate name to find each one.

**A container is basically a lookup table.** Each token is a key, and each key leads to exactly one object:

| Token (key) | What the container hands back |
|---|---|
| `PRISMA_CLIENT` | the database client |
| `EVENT_TYPE_REPOSITORY` | an `EventTypeRepository` |
| `EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_REPOSITORY` | an `EventTypeFavoriteRepository`, which reads and writes favorite rows |
| `EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE` | an `EventTypeFavoriteService`, which runs the access check and then calls the repositories (**new**) |

The repository and the service are different classes doing different jobs, so they need different keys. If they shared one key, asking for it would return only one of them.

**Here's what happens when the tRPC handler calls `getEventTypeFavoriteService()`:**

```
container.get(EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE)
  └─ recipe: "new EventTypeFavoriteService({ eventTypeFavoriteRepository, eventTypeRepository })"
       ├─ needs eventTypeFavoriteRepository → container.get(EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_REPOSITORY)
       │     └─ recipe: "new EventTypeFavoriteRepository(prisma)" → container.get(PRISMA_CLIENT)
       └─ needs eventTypeRepository → container.get(EVENT_TYPE_REPOSITORY)
             └─ recipe: "new EventTypeRepository(prisma)" → container.get(PRISMA_CLIENT)
```

Every arrow is the container looking something up **by its token**. That's why the repository token still matters even though the handler never asks for it directly: the service's recipe uses it to say "give me the favorites repository." Without `EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_REPOSITORY`, the service would have no way to ask for its dependency.

**Who asks for each token:**
- `EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE` is asked for by `getEventTypeFavoriteService()`, which the tRPC handlers will call.
- `EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_REPOSITORY` is asked for by the service's recipe (step 6), and by `getEventTypeFavoriteRepository()` for your integration test.

**And the `_MODULE` tokens?** Those name the *recipes* rather than the objects. The container uses them to keep track of which recipes it has already loaded, so calling the getter repeatedly doesn't register duplicates. Every buildable thing gets that pair (object token plus module token), which is why the file has two pairs.

Does that clear it up? If so, reply **"approve 3"**.

The tRPC handler (the endpoint) calls `getEventTypeFavoriteService()`, which uses the token to get the service from the container. Then the handler calls `.setFavorite(...)` or `.listFavoriteIds(...)` on it.
- **`EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_REPOSITORY` *is* one of the dependencies; it doesn't build them.** The **container** does the building. When it builds the service, it looks up this token to get the repository the service needs, and passes it in.

In one sentence: the endpoint asks for the **service** by its token, and the container uses the **repository's** token to fill in what the service needs.

```ts
13    constructor(private readonly deps: IEventTypeFavoriteServiceDeps) {}
14
15    async setFavorite({ userId, eventTypeId, isFavorite }: SetFavoriteInput): Promise<void> {
16      // Removing only deletes the caller's own row, so it needs no access check. This also lets
17      // users clear favorites for event types they've since lost access to.
18      if (!isFavorite) {
19        await this.deps.eventTypeFavoriteRepository.delete({ userId, eventTypeId });
20        return;
21      }
22
23      const hasAccess = await this.deps.eventTypeRepository.existsWithUserAccess({ id: eventTypeId, userId });
24      // Same error for "doesn't exist" and "not yours" so callers can't probe for other users' event type IDs
25      if (!hasAccess) {
26        throw ErrorWithCode.Factory.EventTypeNotFound(`Event type ${eventTypeId} not found`);
27      }
28
29      await this.deps.eventTypeFavoriteRepository.create({ userId, eventTypeId });
```

### Imports (1–3)

- **1:** `ErrorWithCode` is the error class the repo's rules require outside tRPC routers. It's a normal (not type-only) import because line 26 actually creates an error at runtime.
- **2–3:** `import type` brings in only the *types* of the two repositories, not their code. The service never calls `new` on a repository; the container hands them in already built, so the service only needs to know their shape. This keeps the service free of Prisma: neither import pulls in database code. The relative paths (`../repositories/...`) match how `EventTypeService.ts` imports its repository. Note that `eventTypeRepository` really is lowercase on disk.

### The dependency list (5–8)

- **5:** `interface IEventTypeFavoriteServiceDeps` describes everything the service needs from outside. `export` makes it available to the test file (step 5). The `I...Deps` name follows the example in `patterns-dependency-injection.md`.
- **6–7:** the two dependencies.
  - **These key names matter:** in step 6, `bindModuleToClassOnToken` reads this interface, and TypeScript requires the module's `depsMap` to have exactly these keys, `eventTypeFavoriteRepository` and `eventTypeRepository`. If the module misses one or misspells it, the build fails. That's the "type-safe DI" the rules describe.

### Input type (10)

- **10:** `SetFavoriteInput` names the shape of `setFavorite`'s argument. It's exported so the tRPC handler (step 9) and the test can use the same type instead of repeating it.
  - Why `userId` is a parameter rather than read from a session inside the service: the service doesn't know about logins. The handler passes `ctx.user.id`. This keeps the service usable from tRPC, API v2 or tests.

### Class and constructor (12–13)

- **12:** `export class EventTypeFavoriteService` is the name that step 6 binds and step 7's getter returns.
- **13:** `constructor(private readonly deps: ...) {}` is TypeScript shorthand that declares a `deps` property and assigns it in one go, which is why the body is empty `{}`.
  - `private` means only this class can reach `this.deps`.
  - `readonly` means nothing can swap the dependencies after construction.
  - One `deps` object rather than two separate arguments is what `bindModuleToClassOnToken`'s `depsMap` mode expects: it calls `new EventTypeFavoriteService({ eventTypeFavoriteRepository, eventTypeRepository })`.

### `setFavorite` (15–30)

- **15:** `async` because it awaits the database. The argument is unpacked right in the signature, and it returns `Promise<void>` because the caller already knows what it asked for; the handler echoes the input back in step 9.
- **16–17:** a *why* comment, since the early exit for removal is a deliberate decision that isn't obvious from the code.
- **18–21:** **the unfavorite path, handled first as an early return.**
  - `delete` uses `deleteMany` with `{ userId, eventTypeId }`, so it can only ever delete *this user's* row. The worst case is a no-op.
  - `return` on line 20 stops here, so the rest of the method only deals with adding. This follows the repo's early-return rule and avoids an `if/else` with nesting.
- **23:** **the access check**, which is the step 1 method. Note the mapping `{ id: eventTypeId, userId }`: the repository calls it `id` because it's a generic event type method.
- **24:** a *why* comment explaining the identical-error choice we discussed.
- **25–27:** **an early exit when there's no access.**
  - `ErrorWithCode.Factory.EventTypeNotFound(...)` creates an `ErrorWithCode` with code `EventTypeNotFound`. `errorConversionMiddleware`, already on `authedProcedure`, converts it to HTTP 404, then tRPC `NOT_FOUND` (`getServerErrorFromUnknown.ts:170-173`).
  - The message contains only the ID the user sent, so it reveals nothing new.
  - `throw` stops execution, so line 29 never runs and nothing is written.
- **29:** **the favorite path.** We only get here if `isFavorite` is `true` and access passed. `create` uses `createMany` with `skipDuplicates`, so starring something already starred is harmless.

### `listFavoriteIds` (32–34)

- **32:** takes `{ userId }` as an object, consistent with `setFavorite` and the repository style. It returns `Promise<number[]>`, the event type IDs.
- **33:** passes straight through to your repository method, which returns them newest first. There's no access check here: it only returns *this user's own* favorites, and the UI ignores IDs that don't match a card on the page.
  - **Why it's still in the service and not called directly by the handler:** handlers only talk to the service. If the read side ever needs logic (for example, filtering out event types the user lost access to), it goes here without touching the tRPC layer.

### What's deliberately missing

- No Prisma, no `TRPCError`, no session or `ctx` handling. Those belong to the layers above and below.
- No `try/catch`. Errors pass up to the middleware, which handles them.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-08 06:24:07Z)**_

Yes. To be precise, the work is split across three layers:

```
tRPC handler  →  EventTypeFavoriteService  →  repositories  →  Prisma / Postgres
(who's asking)   (the rules)                  (the queries)
```

- **The service holds the rules:** check access before adding, skip the check when removing, and return the same error for "doesn't exist" and "not yours."
- **The service doesn't contain queries either.** It asks the repositories for data (`existsWithUserAccess`, `create`, `delete`, `findEventTypeIdsByUserId`), and only the repositories talk to Prisma.
- **The handlers will only know** "call `setFavorite` or `listFavoriteIds` with the logged-in user's ID." They never see a query or a rule.

The payoff: if the database layer changes, only the repositories change. If the rules change, only the service changes. And any caller, whether tRPC today or API v2 later, gets the same behavior.

```typescript
import { ErrorWithCode } from "@calcom/lib/errors";
import type { EventTypeFavoriteRepository } from "../repositories/EventTypeFavoriteRepository";
import type { EventTypeRepository } from "../repositories/eventTypeRepository";

export interface IEventTypeFavoriteServiceDeps {
  eventTypeFavoriteRepository: EventTypeFavoriteRepository;
  eventTypeRepository: EventTypeRepository;
}

export type SetFavoriteInput = { userId: number; eventTypeId: number; isFavorite: boolean };

export class EventTypeFavoriteService {
  constructor(private readonly deps: IEventTypeFavoriteServiceDeps) {}

  async setFavorite({ userId, eventTypeId, isFavorite }: SetFavoriteInput): Promise<void> {
    // Removing only deletes the caller's own row, so it needs no access check. This also lets
    // users clear favorites for event types they've since lost access to.
    if (!isFavorite) {
      await this.deps.eventTypeFavoriteRepository.delete({ userId, eventTypeId });
      return;
    }

    const hasAccess = await this.deps.eventTypeRepository.existsWithUserAccess({ id: eventTypeId, userId });
    // Same error for "doesn't exist" and "not yours" so callers can't probe for other users' event type IDs
    if (!hasAccess) {
      throw ErrorWithCode.Factory.EventTypeNotFound(`Event type ${eventTypeId} not found`);
    }

    await this.deps.eventTypeFavoriteRepository.create({ userId, eventTypeId });
  }

  async listFavoriteIds({ userId }: { userId: number }): Promise<number[]> {
    return this.deps.eventTypeFavoriteRepository.findEventTypeIdsByUserId(userId);
  }
}
```

## Step 6: The service's DI module (the "recipe")

**New file:** `packages/features/eventtypes/di/EventTypeFavoriteService.module.ts`. It follows the same structure as your `EventTypeFavoriteRepository.module.ts`. The difference is that it has two dependencies (`depsMap`) instead of one (`dep`).

```ts
 1  import { bindModuleToClassOnToken, createModule, type ModuleLoader } from "@calcom/features/di/di";
 2  import { moduleLoader as eventTypeRepositoryModuleLoader } from "@calcom/features/di/modules/EventType";
 3  import { DI_TOKENS } from "@calcom/features/di/tokens";
 4  import { EventTypeFavoriteService } from "../service/EventTypeFavoriteService";
 5  import { moduleLoader as eventTypeFavoriteRepositoryModuleLoader } from "./EventTypeFavoriteRepository.module";
 6
 7  const thisModule = createModule();
 8  const token = DI_TOKENS.EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE;
 9  const moduleToken = DI_TOKENS.EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE_MODULE;
10
11  const loadModule = bindModuleToClassOnToken({
12    module: thisModule,
13    moduleToken,
14    token,
15    classs: EventTypeFavoriteService,
16    depsMap: {
17      eventTypeFavoriteRepository: eventTypeFavoriteRepositoryModuleLoader,
18      eventTypeRepository: eventTypeRepositoryModuleLoader,
19    },
20  });
21
22  export const moduleLoader: ModuleLoader = {
23    token,
24    loadModule,
25  };
26
27  export type { EventTypeFavoriteService };
```

### Imports (1–5)

- **1:** three DI helpers from the repo's wrapper around the `@evyweb/ioctopus` library:
  - `createModule` makes an empty recipe book;
  - `bindModuleToClassOnToken` writes a type-checked recipe into it;
  - `ModuleLoader` is the type for the `{ token, loadModule }` object we export.

  `type ModuleLoader` inside the braces marks just that one name as type-only.
- **2:** the **existing** module (recipe) for `EventTypeRepository`. We don't write a recipe for it; we reuse the one in `di/modules/EventType.ts`. `as eventTypeRepositoryModuleLoader` renames it on import, because every module file exports something called `moduleLoader`, and two imports with the same name would clash.
- **3:** `DI_TOKENS` is the global token list, which includes the two tokens from step 3 through the spread.
- **4:** a **real** (not type-only) import of the service class. The container needs the actual class to call `new` on it.
- **5:** **your** repository module, with the same renaming as line 2. A relative path because it's in the same folder.

### Setup (7–9)

- **7:** `thisModule` is the empty recipe book for this service.
- **8:** `token` is the name the built service will be stored under (step 3's `EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE`).
- **9:** `moduleToken` is the name the recipe itself is filed under, so loading it again doesn't create duplicates.

### The recipe (11–20)

- **11:** `bindModuleToClassOnToken` writes the recipe and returns `loadModule`, the function that installs it into a container.
- **12–14:** which recipe book to write in and which names to use. `moduleToken,` is shorthand for `moduleToken: moduleToken`.
- **15:** `classs: EventTypeFavoriteService` is the class to build. It's spelled with three s's on purpose, because `class` is a reserved word in JavaScript.
- **16–19:** **`depsMap`** maps each constructor dependency to the recipe that builds it.
  - **The keys** (`eventTypeFavoriteRepository`, `eventTypeRepository`) must match the fields of `IEventTypeFavoriteServiceDeps` from step 4 exactly. TypeScript checks this. If you add a third dependency to the service and forget it here, the build fails. That's the type safety the DI rule talks about.
  - **The values** are the recipes that build each dependency. Internally (`di/di.ts:113-114`), the helper turns this into "build the service with `{ eventTypeFavoriteRepository: <thing under EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_REPOSITORY>, eventTypeRepository: <thing under EVENT_TYPE_REPOSITORY> }`."
  - **Why `depsMap` and not `dep`:** your repository module uses `dep` because the repository's constructor takes *one* thing, the Prisma client. The service's constructor takes *one object with two fields*, which is what `depsMap` is for.
- **20:** closes the call.

### What happens when `loadModule` runs (behind the scenes, `di/di.ts:117-131`)

1. It installs this recipe into the container.
2. It loops over `depsMap` and installs each dependency's recipe: your repository module, which also installs Prisma through its own `dep`, and the `EventType` module.

So installing the service's recipe installs everything it needs. That's what lets the getter in step 7 be one line.

### Exports (22–27)

- **22–25:** `moduleLoader` is the object other files use: the token to ask for, plus the function that installs the recipe.
  - `: ModuleLoader` matches your `EventTypeFavoriteRepository.module.ts`. (`EventTypeService.module.ts` uses `satisfies ModuleLoader` instead; both are fine. I picked the one your sibling file uses so the two favorites modules look the same.)
- **27:** `export type { EventTypeFavoriteService }` re-exports the class **as a type only**. Step 7's container imports it from here to declare `getEventTypeFavoriteService(): EventTypeFavoriteService`. Callers get the return type without importing the service file directly. Your repository module does the same on its last line.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-08 07:00:51Z)**_

**Mostly yes, with two corrections.** Here's what the code shows across all 87 DI module files in `packages/features`.

**1. "One class = one recipe module": confirmed as the convention.**
- 83 of 87 module files bind exactly one thing.
- Only four bind more than one:
  - `Webhook.module.ts` (10)
  - `Watchlist.module.ts` (5)
  - `Webhook.service.ts` (4)
  - `Prisma.ts` (2: the normal and the read-only client, which are one concept)

  The webhook and watchlist exceptions are older grouped designs, not the pattern to copy. The rules doc (`patterns-dependency-injection.md`) shows one class per `.module.ts`, which is what we're doing: your repository module and the service module in step 6 are separate files.

**2. "Each layer is self-contained": the target, but not universal, and it's per module rather than per layer.**
- **It's per module, not per layer.** Each module declares its own dependencies and installs them when it loads. That's what `bindModuleToClassOnToken` does: 54 of the module files use it. So the service's recipe automatically installs your repository's recipe, which installs Prisma's. Nothing about "repository layer" or "service layer" is bundled together; each recipe just brings its own dependencies.
- **Not universal.** 18 module files use the older raw `.bind(...).toClass(...)` style, which **doesn't** install its own dependencies. `di/modules/EventType.ts`, which our service uses, is one of them. It needs Prisma but never loads it. That's why the plan has step 7's container load Prisma explicitly, as `EventTypeService.container.ts` does, rather than relying on luck.

**So for our files:**
- your repository module follows both conventions;
- the step 6 service module follows both conventions;
- one dependency (`EventType`) doesn't, and step 7 works around that.

Step 6 is written. That leaves **step 7**, which is the combined, renamed container you chose. It's the last step of Phase 1, and it touches two files.

## Step 7: Rename the container and add the service getter

### 7a. Rename the file
```bash
git mv packages/features/eventtypes/di/EventTypeFavoriteRepository.container.ts \
       packages/features/eventtypes/di/EventTypeFavorite.container.ts
```
`git mv` renames the file and tells Git it's a rename, so the file's history stays connected and the PR diff shows "renamed" plus the edits, not a delete and a new file. The only importer is the integration test (7c).

### 7b. Contents of `EventTypeFavorite.container.ts` after the rename

Lines marked **new** are additions. Lines marked **changed** are existing lines I'd edit. Everything else, including your comments, is unchanged.


**Line by line (new and changed only):**

- **2:** `prismaModule` is the Prisma recipe book itself. We need the module object here, not its `moduleLoader`, because line 18 loads it by hand. `EventTypeService.container.ts:2` imports it the same way.
- **3:** `DI_TOKENS`, for `PRISMA_MODULE` on line 18.
- **9–12:** the step 6 module.
  - `type EventTypeFavoriteService` is the type-only re-export from step 6's last line. It's used for the getter's return type on line 32, without loading the service file twice.
  - `moduleLoader as eventTypeFavoriteServiceModuleLoader` is renamed so it doesn't clash with the repository's `moduleLoader` on line 7.
- **15 (changed):** renames the variable from `eventTypeFavoriteRepositoryContainer` to `eventTypeFavoriteContainer`, because it now holds the repository **and** the service. The old name would mislead. This is the same reason you chose the file rename. Created once at the top of the file, so both getters share it.
- **16–17:** a *why* comment. Without it, line 18 looks redundant, and someone might delete it.
- **18:** installs Prisma's recipe into the container under `PRISMA_MODULE`.
  - **Why it's needed:** the service needs `EventTypeRepository`, and `di/modules/EventType.ts` is one of the 18 older modules that **doesn't** load its own dependencies. Without line 18, `EventTypeRepository` would only find Prisma because your favorites repository module (step 6, line 17) happens to load it first. If someone later reordered `depsMap` or removed the favorites repository, it would break at runtime.
  - **Why it's safe:** your repository module also loads Prisma under the same `PRISMA_MODULE` key, and the container just files it under that key again. `EventTypeService.container.ts:11` does exactly this.
- **24, 27 (changed):** the only edits to your existing function are the new variable name. Its behavior is identical.
- **32:** the new getter, which the tRPC handlers will call. The return type comes from line 10.
- **33:** installs the service's recipe. As covered in step 6, this also installs both repository recipes. It runs on every call, which is the standard pattern; repeated loads simply replace the same entries.
- **34:** asks the container for the object stored under `EVENT_TYPE_FAVORITE_SERVICE`. The first time, the container builds `EventTypeFavoriteRepository(prisma)`, then `EventTypeRepository(prisma)`, then `new EventTypeFavoriteService({ ... })`, and hands it back. `<EventTypeFavoriteService>` tells TypeScript what comes back.

I left out comments on the new getter, to match `EventTypeService.container.ts` and the repo's no-"what"-comments rule. The blank line at 25 also drops the trailing spaces that were on the old line 16, which Biome flagged earlier.

**One optional change to your comment (line 20):** it says API routes call `getEventTypeFavoriteRepository`, but after this PR they'll call `getEventTypeFavoriteService`, and the repository getter will only be used by the integration test. If you'd like it accurate, I'd replace lines 20–21 with:
```ts
// app code should use getEventTypeFavoriteService; this getter exists so the integration test
// can exercise the repository's DI wiring against a real database
```
If you'd rather keep your original comment, say so.

### 7c. Integration test: line 2

```ts
import { getEventTypeFavoriteRepository } from "@calcom/features/eventtypes/di/EventTypeFavorite.container";
```
Only the file name in the path changes (`EventTypeFavoriteRepository.container` becomes `EventTypeFavorite.container`). Without this, the import would point at a file that no longer exists and the test wouldn't load.

```typescript
} from "./EventTypeFavoriteRepository.module";
import {
  type EventTypeFavoriteService,
  moduleLoader as eventTypeFavoriteServiceModuleLoader,
} from "./EventTypeFavoriteService.module";

// created once the file is imported so all function calls share the same same container
const eventTypeFavoriteContainer = createContainer();
// EventType's repository module doesn't load Prisma itself; without this the service

eventTypeFavoriteContainer.load(DI_TOKENS.PRISMA_MODULE, prismaModule);

export function getEventTypeFavoriteRepository(): EventTypeFavoriteRepository {

  // uses the key to find the module (instructions), builds the repository with Prisma, and returns it.
  return eventTypeFavoriteContainer.get<EventTypeFavoriteRepository>(
    eventTypeFavoriteRepositoryModuleLoader.token
  );
}

export function getEventTypeFavoriteService(): EventTypeFavoriteService {
  eventTypeFavoriteServiceModuleLoader.loadModule(eventTypeFavoriteContainer);
  return eventTypeFavoriteContainer.get<EventTypeFavoriteService>(eventTypeFavoriteServiceModuleLoader.token);
}
```

## Phase 2, step 8: `setFavorite` input schema

**New file:** `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/eventTypes/setFavorite.schema.ts`, in the same shape as [delete.schema.ts](packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/eventTypes/delete.schema.ts):

```ts
 1  import { z } from "zod";
 2
 3  export type TSetFavoriteInputSchema = {
 4    eventTypeId: number;
 5    isFavorite: boolean;
 6  };
 7
 8  export const ZSetFavoriteInputSchema: z.ZodType<TSetFavoriteInputSchema> = z.object({
 9    eventTypeId: z.number().int().positive(),
10    isFavorite: z.boolean(),
11  });
```

**Line by line:**

- **1:** `z` from Zod, the validation library tRPC uses. tRPC runs every incoming request through the procedure's schema *before* the handler runs, so bad input never reaches the service.
- **3–6:** `TSetFavoriteInputSchema` is the TypeScript type of valid input. The handler (step 9) uses it to type its `input`.
  - Why write it out by hand instead of deriving it with `z.infer`: that's the style of `delete.schema.ts`. Line 8 then ties the two together, so they can't drift apart: if the type and the schema disagree, TypeScript errors.
  - **There's no `userId` field, deliberately.** The user ID comes from the logged-in session (`ctx.user.id`) in the handler, so a client can't send someone else's ID. With no field for it, it's impossible to even try.
- **8:** `ZSetFavoriteInputSchema` is the schema object the router (step 11) passes to `.input(...)`.
  - The `Z` prefix is the repo's naming convention for schemas, and `T` is for types; compare `ZDeleteInputSchema` and `TDeleteInputSchema`.
  - The annotation `: z.ZodType<TSetFavoriteInputSchema>` is what forces the schema's output to match the type from lines 3–6.
  - `z.object({...})` means the input must be an object with these fields. By default, Zod quietly drops any extra fields a client sends, so they never reach the handler.
- **9:** `eventTypeId` must be a number (`z.number()`), a whole number (`.int()`, which rejects `4.5`), and greater than 0 (`.positive()`, which rejects `0` and `-1`). Event type IDs are database auto-increment integers starting at 1, so anything else is malformed and gets rejected with `BAD_REQUEST` before any database work. `delete.schema.ts` only uses `z.number()`; the extra two checks are cheap and stop pointless queries.
- **10:** `isFavorite` must be exactly `true` or `false`. Strings like `"true"` or numbers like `1` are rejected. This is the explicit "set to" value rather than a toggle, which is what makes repeated clicks safe.

Correct. Each layer has one job:

| Layer | Its job | In our code |
|---|---|---|
| **tRPC** (handler and router) | Accept the request, validate the input, get the logged-in user, call the service, return the result | steps 8–11 |
| **Service** | Business rules: check access before adding, skip the check when removing, use one error for "missing" and "not yours" | `EventTypeFavoriteService` |
| **Repository** | Database queries, and nothing else | `EventTypeFavoriteRepository`, `existsWithUserAccess` |

So the tRPC handler never runs a query **and** never makes a rule decision. It's only the doorway. The service decides; the repositories do the actual reading and writing.

One extra benefit: since the rules live in the service rather than in tRPC, any other entry point (API v2, a background job) can call the same service and get identical behavior without copying the logic.

- **3:** `TrpcSessionUser` is the type of the logged-in user tRPC puts on `ctx`. Type-only, because we only use it to describe the argument.
- **4:** the input type from step 8.
- **6–11:** `SetFavoriteOptions` describes what the router passes in. It's the same shape as `DeleteOptions` in `delete.handler.ts`.

Almost. The handler is the code the entry point **runs**. The entry point itself is the router entry in `_router.ts`, which is step 11. Here's the order a request goes through:

```
Frontend: trpc.viewer.eventTypes.setFavorite.useMutation()
   ↓
1. _router.ts → setFavorite: authedProcedure ...   ← the entry point (step 11)
     • authedProcedure: rejects logged-out users, sets up error conversion
     • .input(ZSetFavoriteInputSchema): validates the input (step 8)
   ↓
2. setFavorite.handler.ts → setFavoriteHandler     ← what the entry point runs (step 9)
     • takes ctx.user.id from the session, calls the service
   ↓
3. EventTypeFavoriteService → repositories → database
```

The router entry gives the endpoint its **name** (`setFavorite`, which the frontend calls as `trpc.viewer.eventTypes.setFavorite`) and its **gatekeeping**: login required, input validated. The handler then contains what happens once a request gets through.

They're separate files because the router loads each handler only when it's first called, with `await import("./setFavorite.handler")`. That keeps the router file small and app start-up fast, and every procedure in this router works the same way.

  - **`async ({ ctx, input }) =>`** receives the logged-in context and the already-validated input.
- **3:** **loads the handler on demand.** `await import(...)` loads `setFavorite.handler.ts` the first time this procedure is called, not when the server starts. Every procedure in this file does this (for example, `delete` at lines 107–110). It keeps start-up light; the module is cached after the first load. The `{ setFavoriteHandler }` destructuring picks the exported function out of the loaded module.
- **5–8:** calls the handler and returns its result (`{ eventTypeId, isFavorite }`) to the frontend. The multi-line `{ ctx, input }` matches this file's formatting.
- **9:** closes the procedure. The trailing comma separates it from the next entry.
- **11:** **the `listFavoriteIds` entry point.**
  - **No `.input(...)`**: the query takes nothing from the client. This is the same shape as `list` and `listWithTeam` at lines 86–100.
  - **`.query(...)`** marks it as a **read**. On the frontend that means `useQuery`, which runs when the page loads, caches the result, and can be refreshed after a `setFavorite` succeeds.
  - It only receives `ctx`, since there's no input.
- **12:** loads `listFavoriteIds.handler.ts` on demand, the same as line 3.
- **14–16:** calls the handler with only `ctx` and returns `{ eventTypeIds }`.

**Placement:** both go at the end, together, so the favorites procedures are easy to find and the diff is one clean block. Putting them elsewhere (for example, next to `list`) would work the same.

- `yarn type-check:ci --force` (the full repo check the rules require before pushing; this takes a few minutes);
- Biome on the new tRPC files.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-08 07:56:56Z)**_

Correct. `setFavorite` handles both directions through `isFavorite`:

- `{ eventTypeId: 42, isFavorite: true }` checks access, then adds the row.
- `{ eventTypeId: 42, isFavorite: false }` removes the row, with no access check (the early return in the service).

That was a deliberate choice over separate `addFavorite` and `deleteFavorite` endpoints:
- **The UI sends the state it wants, not an action.** The star button simply sends `!currentlyStarred`.
- **Repeats are safe.** Sending `false` twice deletes once and then does nothing, and sending `true` twice is skipped by `skipDuplicates`. A toggle endpoint would flip back on a double click.
- **Less code:** one schema, one handler and one router entry instead of two of each.

```text
    if (!pages) return;
    const newOrder = pages;
    const pageNo = Math.floor(index / LIMIT);

      increment === -1

    }

    mutation.mutate({
      ids: newOrder.flatMap((page) => page.eventTypes.map((type) => type.id)),
    });
  }
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-08 08:00:51Z)**_

The dilemma comes from how this page loads cards today. Here is what I found in [event-types-listing-view.tsx](apps/web/modules/event-types/views/event-types-listing-view.tsx), and what it means for the Favorites section.

## How the page loads cards today

- **10 at a time.** `LIMIT = 10` ([line 71](apps/web/modules/event-types/views/event-types-listing-view.tsx#L71)). The page calls `getEventTypesFromGroup` as an "infinite query" ([line 119](apps/web/modules/event-types/views/event-types-listing-view.tsx#L119)). The first request returns cards 1–10, sorted by `position`.
- **More load as you scroll.** A "Load more" button sits at the bottom. When it scrolls into view, the next 10 load automatically ([lines 136–139](apps/web/modules/event-types/views/event-types-listing-view.tsx#L136-L139)).
- **Each tab is its own list.** Your personal event types and each team are separate tabs, with separate requests and separate pages.
- **Search runs on the server.** The search box filters which cards come back.

The browser only ever holds the cards that have loaded so far.

## Problem 1: favorites that haven't loaded yet

`listFavoriteIds` returns **IDs only**, like `[18, 3]`. To draw a card in the Favorites section, the page needs the card's full data: title, slug, length, hidden state, hosts and so on. That data only arrives with the page of 10 the card belongs to.

**Example:** you have 25 event types and star #18, which sits on page 2 by position.
1. You open the page. Page 1 loads (cards 1–10). The page knows 18 is a favorite but has no card data for it, so **the Favorites section is missing it.**
2. You scroll down and page 2 loads. Card 18 suddenly **jumps up** into Favorites.

That breaks the issue's promise that starred cards appear "at the top of the screen." It only happens if you have more than 10 event types in a tab. Below that, everything fits on page 1 and there's no problem.

There's a tab wrinkle too. `listFavoriteIds` returns favorites from **all** tabs, while each tab only loads its own cards. From IDs alone, the page can't tell whether a favorite hasn't loaded yet or belongs to a different tab.

## Problem 2: reordering breaks (applies whichever option you pick)

This one is less obvious. The up and down arrows use `moveEventType` ([lines 364–416](apps/web/modules/event-types/views/event-types-listing-view.tsx#L364-L416)):
- It finds a card by its position in the **loaded pages** (`LIMIT * pageIdx + index`) and swaps it with its neighbor **in those pages**.
- It sends **every loaded ID**, in order, to `eventTypeOrder`, which rewrites the `position` of each one.
- It decides whether to hide the arrows for the first and last cards from the same pages ([lines 522–523](apps/web/modules/event-types/views/event-types-listing-view.tsx#L522-L523)).

Suppose favorites are only *visually* moved out of the regular list but stay in the loaded pages. Then:
- clicking "move up" on a regular card can swap it with a **hidden favorite**, so the card seems not to move;
- the first and last arrows show or hide on the wrong cards.

The issue says users "can continue to rearrange regular events however they like," so this has to work.

## The three ways to solve it

### Option A: split the loaded cards in the browser
- **How it works:** the page fetches `listFavoriteIds` and puts loaded cards whose ID is in the set into Favorites, and the rest below.
- **Changes:** UI only. No backend changes.
- **Problems:**
  - Problem 1 stays: unloaded favorites appear late. Automatically loading more pages until every favorite is found doesn't work either, because of the tab wrinkle: a favorite from another tab would never be found, so it would load the entire list.
  - `moveEventType` has to be rewritten to work only on the regular cards, and that function is already the most fragile code on the page.

### Option B: let the server filter the existing query (recommended)
- **How it works:** add one optional filter to `getEventTypesFromGroup`'s input, for example `favorites: "only" | "exclude"`. The handler gets the user's favorite IDs from your service and adds one condition to its existing database filter: `id: { in: favoriteIds }` for "only", or `id: { notIn: favoriteIds }` for "exclude".
- **What the page does:** it makes two calls per tab:
  - the Favorites section calls with `"only"`;
  - the regular list calls with `"exclude"` and keeps its existing 10-at-a-time loading.
- **Why it solves both problems:**
  - Favorites arrive with full card data on first load, whatever their position.
  - The tab is filtered on the server, so the tab wrinkle disappears.
  - Search still applies to both sections.
  - **The regular list's pages contain no favorites at all**, so `moveEventType`, the arrows and `eventTypeOrder` work **unchanged**. That's the biggest win.
- **Changes:** 2 backend files (`getByViewer.schema.ts` gets the filter; `getEventTypesFromGroup.handler.ts` gets the condition) plus the UI. After a star click succeeds, the page refreshes `getEventTypesFromGroup`, and both sections update.
- **Small costs:**
  - Favorites come back in `position` order. To show newest first, the page re-sorts them using the order from `listFavoriteIds`, which is a few lines.
  - The handler you'd be editing is older code that queries Prisma directly. We'd only add the filter and leave the rest as it is.

### Option C: have the server sort favorites first in one list (not recommended)
- **How it works:** the one existing query returns favorites first, then the rest.
- **Why not:** the 10-at-a-time loading tracks where it left off by card ID, while the list is sorted by `position`. Mixing a second sort key into that is easy to get subtly wrong: cards get duplicated or skipped between pages. And the handler merges two separate database queries before sorting, which makes it worse. Reordering would also still need Problem 2's rewrite.

## Comparison

| | A: browser split | B: server filter | C: server sort |
|---|---|---|---|
| Favorites on unloaded pages | ❌ appear late | ✅ | ✅ |
| Team tabs | ❌ ambiguous | ✅ | ✅ |
| Reordering | needs a rewrite | ✅ unchanged | needs a rewrite |
| Backend changes | none | 2 files, small | 1 file, risky |
| Risk | medium (fragile reorder code) | low | high (paging bugs) |

I'd go with **Option B**. It adds two backend files to an already large PR, but it's the only option that meets the issue's "at the top" promise for every user, and it leaves the delicate reordering code untouched. Option A is only worth it if keeping backend changes out of the UI work matters more to you than late-appearing favorites, which only affect tabs with more than 10 event types.

Tell me which way you want to go, and I'll plan Phase 3 around it, file by file as before.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-08 08:17:08Z)**_

Partly. Two calls is how B works, but it isn't *why* B is best. In fact, Option A also makes two calls: one to `getEventTypesFromGroup` and one to `listFavoriteIds`.

The real difference is **who does the splitting, and how much data they have to do it with**:

- **In A, the browser splits**, and it only sees the cards loaded so far. So it can miss favorites, and favorites stay mixed into the pages the reorder code relies on.
- **In B, the server splits**, and it sees all of the user's event types in that tab. So:
  - the Favorites call returns **every** favorite, complete, on first load;
  - the regular call returns **only** non-favorites, so the reorder code never encounters a favorite and doesn't need to change.

The key idea is that **each section gets its own complete, correct list from the server**, rather than one list the browser has to cut apart. The two calls are just what that requires.

Do you want me to plan Phase 3 with Option B?

<summary>Tool use: **AskUserQuestion**</summary>
**With Option B, the page knows a card is starred simply by which section it's in (the Favorites call only returns favorites). That means the UI never needs the listFavoriteIds endpoint we built in steps 10–11. The getEventTypesFromGroup handler will still use the service's listFavoriteIds method internally. What should happen to the endpoint?**

Options:
- **Remove it (Recommended)** - Delete listFavoriteIds.handler.ts and its router entry. No dead code ships, and the PR has one less file. The service method stays because the handler uses it.
- **Keep it** - Leave the endpoint in place for possible future use (e.g., a favorites widget elsewhere). It ships unused in this PR.

**How should the Favorites section behave?**

Options:
- **No reordering (Recommended)** - Favorites show in the same position order they had in the regular list, with no up/down arrows. The issue only requires reordering regular events, and reordering favorites would rewrite positions that the regular list also uses.
- **Reorderable** - Up/down arrows inside Favorites too. Moving a favorite rewrites its position, so when it is unstarred it may land somewhere unexpected in the regular list.


**Answer:** Remove it (Recommended), No reordering (Recommended)
</details></tool-use>

```text
## Approved Plan:
# Plan: Favorite event types (Option A: service layer)

## Context

On the Event Types page, a user can star an event type to move it into a Favorites section at the top, and unstar it to send it back to the regular list. The `EventTypeFavorite` table, `EventTypeFavoriteRepository`, and its DI container already exist and are tested, but nothing calls them yet.

This branch becomes **one PR**, built in three phases:
1. a service with DI;
2. tRPC procedures (`setFavorite`, `listFavoriteIds`);
3. the UI.

Phases 1–2 are implemented. Phase 3 (below) uses Option B: the server splits favorites from regular event types.

## Working agreement

For every file, in order:
1. Show the full proposed code (or the exact lines inserted), with line numbers, and explain each line in depth.
2. **Wait for explicit approval** before writing anything.
3. Write exactly what was approved. If the user asks for changes, revise, re-explain, and wait again.

No commits, pushes, or PRs unless asked. Step 0 creates a branch (we're on `main`), and that also needs approval.

## Design decisions

- **Access rule:** a user can favorite an event type if they own it, are assigned to it, host it, or are an *accepted* member of its team. This is the rule from `eventTypeOrder.handler.ts:18-46` plus `hosts`.
- **Don't use `createEventPbacProcedure`:** it checks edit rights, and its `PermissionCheckService` is a stub that always returns `true` (`util.ts:15-20`).
- **Access checked only when adding:** removing only deletes the caller's own row, so it's always safe, and it lets users clear stale favorites.
- **`ErrorWithCode.Factory.NotFound`, not `Forbidden`:** the error doesn't confirm that someone else's event type exists. `errorConversionMiddleware` (already on `authedProcedure`) maps it to tRPC `NOT_FOUND`.
- **Input is `{ eventTypeId, isFavorite }`, not a toggle:** setting an explicit value is safe to repeat on double clicks and retries.
- **`userId` always comes from `ctx.user.id`:** never from client input.
- **The container loads Prisma explicitly:** `di/modules/EventType.ts` doesn't load it itself. This matches `EventTypeService.container.ts`.

## Phase 1: features layer

## Phase 3: UI with Option B (server-side split)

**Approach:** `getEventTypesFromGroup` gains an optional `favorites: "only" | "exclude"` filter. Each tab makes two calls:
- the Favorites section asks for `"only"`;
- the regular list asks for `"exclude"`.

Each section gets a complete list from the server. Favorites show up on first load whatever their position, and the regular list's pages contain no favorites, so `moveEventType`, the arrows and `eventTypeOrder` keep working unchanged.

**Decisions (user-approved):**
- **Remove the `listFavoriteIds` endpoint.** The UI knows a card's star state from the section it's in. The service's `listFavoriteIds` method stays, because the handler uses it.
- **No reordering in Favorites.** Favorites show in `position` order, with no arrows. Reordering favorites would rewrite positions the regular list also uses.
- **Refresh by invalidating, not an optimistic move.** After `setFavorite` succeeds, invalidate `getEventTypesFromGroup`, and both sections refetch. Moving a card between two paginated caches optimistically is complex and fragile. The star is disabled while the request is pending.
- **The star shows on every card, including read-only team cards.** Favoriting is personal and doesn't edit the event type. It sits before the title, outside the desktop-only and mobile-only containers, so one button covers both layouts.

|---|---|---|

| 14 | `trpc/.../eventTypes/getEventTypesFromGroup.handler.ts` | If `favorites` is set, get the IDs via `getEventTypeFavoriteService().listFavoriteIds({ userId })`, build `{ id: { in \| notIn: ids } }`, and spread it into `baseQueryConditions` (personal) and the team `where`. Both repository methods merge `where` with `...where` (`eventTypeRepository.ts:241-298`, `:509-512`). Empty IDs work naturally: `in: []` returns nothing and `notIn: []` returns everything.
```
